title: Solidarity in Social and Political Philosophy

summaries.example: Imagine two cyclists. One cyclist falls and cannot lift the bicycle alone. The other stops, helps, and thinks, “We are both cyclists, so I should help.” This is a small example of solidarity among people who see themselves as part of the same group. Solidarity can also mean supporting people outside our group, such as helping a community after a disaster. Philosophers disagree about whether that one-way help should always be called solidarity.
summaries.summary: Solidarity is a relationship of unity and shared responsibility. People may feel solidarity because they share a group, a job, an experience, a problem, or a goal. They may help each other, make sacrifices, trust one another, or act together. The idea became especially important when older ties such as family, church, and local work groups were weakened by industrial and market society. Socialists used solidarity to describe workers joining together. Civic thinkers connected it to citizens supporting shared institutions, such as help during sickness or unemployment. Nationalists connected it to a people sharing a history and a common project. Christian thinkers connected it to human interdependence and duties to others. Modern social movements use solidarity while debating what should unite people: shared identity, shared oppression, shared experience, or commitment to a cause. Solidarity can make joint action stronger and help vulnerable people. Yet unity can also threaten freedom, encourage untrue stories, or treat outsiders unfairly. The entry presents these disagreements without claiming that one answer settles them all.
key_ideas: Solidarity means more than simply being in the same place. It usually includes caring, helping, trust, or a shared purpose.
Some philosophers focus on solidarity among members of one group. Others focus on solidarity with people outside one’s group.
Solidarity has been important in workers’ movements, welfare programs, nations, religious thought, and social movements.
Solidarity can help people protect one another and reach goals, but it can also leave outsiders out or support harmful causes.
Philosophers ask whether solidarity is valuable by itself, useful because of what it achieves, or both.
summaries.why_it_matters: Solidarity affects how people respond to unfairness, danger, illness, poverty, and other shared problems. It helps explain why workers form unions, why citizens support public programs, and why people join movements for change. Thinking carefully about solidarity can help us ask who belongs, who gets support, whose voice guides a movement, and whether a group’s goal is just.

important_terms.definition: A special kind of unity in which people support one another or work together because they see a connection between them.
A group whose members see themselves as belonging together and share some important connection, experience, or goal.
Working together to do something that one person might not be able to do alone.
A difficult problem or harmful situation that people may join together to overcome.

questions_to_think_about: When does helping someone count as solidarity rather than ordinary kindness?
Can a group have solidarity if its goal is unfair or harmful?
Should we help group members first, or should everyone receive equal help?
How can a group stay united while allowing people to disagree?

summaries.example: Suppose students organize a campaign after discovering that some classmates cannot participate in a school activity because of a rule that disadvantages them. Students from outside the affected group may offer support, but a philosophical question remains: are they acting in solidarity if they decide the campaign’s goals for themselves, or should they listen and follow the affected students’ direction? One account emphasizes commitment to the disadvantaged group itself; another emphasizes a shared group identity and mutual action; a stricter account requires people to pursue a shared goal together. The example shows why “support” and “solidarity” are not automatically identical.
summaries.summary: The philosophical study of solidarity asks what kind of relationship it is, what practices express it, and why it matters. At its broadest, solidarity involves a distinctive unity, identification, and readiness to share burdens or support action. One major distinction is between solidarity among members of a group and solidarity with an outgroup. The former is often described as reciprocal: members recognize one another as “one of us” and are prepared to set aside narrow self-interest. The latter may be asymmetric, as when outsiders support a disadvantaged movement. Some theorists regard such support as central to solidarity; others argue that unilateral aid is better described as charity, humanitarian assistance, or support for a cause. More demanding accounts require shared goals, trust, loyalty, and coordinated collective action. Other accounts make political opposition to injustice essential, while still others allow solidarity in response to nonpolitical adversity. The history of the concept reflects these tensions. Socialist solidarity centered on workers’ mutual commitment; civic solidarity emphasized citizens’ interdependence and institutions such as welfare provision; national solidarity emphasized a shared historical project; Christian solidarity emphasized obligations arising from human interdependence; and social movements have debated whether solidarity should rest on identity, shared oppression, experience, or a cause. The value of solidarity is also contested. It can help groups coordinate, protect vulnerable members, learn from one another, and challenge oppression. key_ideas: The entry distinguishes solidarity among members of a group from solidarity with an outside group. The first usually involves some symmetry; the second may be one-sided.
Accounts differ over what solidarity requires: identification, mutual aid, shared values, loyalty, trust, opposition to injustice, overcoming adversity, or collective action.
Historically, solidarity has been used in socialism, civic theories of welfare and citizenship, nationalism, Christian social thought, and modern social movements.
Solidarity may have instrumental value because it improves coordination, protects vulnerable members, reduces inequality within a group, and helps people share knowledge.

Some philosophers argue that solidarity can also have non-instrumental value when people jointly realize a just relationship or achieve something worthwhile together, even if they do not fully succeed.

Critics worry that solidarity can suppress liberty, encourage false ideas about what unites a group, or create unfair advantages for insiders. Defenders reply that solidarity can support resistance, democratic institutions, and better understanding of oppression.
summaries.why_it_matters: Solidarity is central to debates about unions, welfare states, nationalism, religion, human rights, and social movements. It helps illuminate how people become capable of collective action and how obligations can arise within groups. At the same time, examining its limits prevents a simple celebration of unity. A serious account must ask whether solidarity respects freedom, includes or excludes outsiders, responds to real injustice, and allows disagreement and diversity.

important_terms.definition: A relation of unity and mutual commitment within a group, or—on some accounts—a committed relation of support between people or groups.
Solidarity understood as a relation among members who identify with the same social group and are prepared to aid one another.
Solidarity understood as support for people or a group with whom the supporter may not share membership; philosophers disagree about whether this is genuine solidarity.
Acting together through mutually coordinated efforts toward a shared aim or against a significant difficulty.
The condition of being connected through mutual dependence, especially within a complex society and its division of labor.
A concern that solidarity is used so broadly that it lacks a coherent or useful meaning.
The objection that solidarity adds nothing important because concepts such as justice, equality, community, or loyalty already do the needed work.
The idea that the value of a practice comes from what it produces, rather than from the practice itself.

questions_to_think_about: What distinguishes solidarity from charity, friendship, loyalty, or ordinary cooperation?
Should a supporter from a more privileged group follow the affected group’s leadership, and why?
Can solidarity exist when the group’s purpose is morally wrong, or should the concept exclude such cases?
Does a nation need shared historical stories to sustain solidarity, and what if those stories are inaccurate?
How should special duties to solidarity partners be limited by wider demands of justice?

summaries.example: A group of students notices that a classmate is being left out of a team activity. They change the rules and share the work so the classmate can take part. If they do this because they see themselves as classmates who should support one another, that may be solidarity among the group. If students from another class join the effort after listening to the excluded student’s concerns, that may be solidarity with the student or group. Philosophers disagree about whether the second case counts as solidarity, especially if the helpers act without sharing the same experience.
summaries.summary: Solidarity is a special kind of togetherness. It can describe people in one group supporting each other, or people supporting a group they do not belong to. Philosophers disagree about which meaning is most important. One view says solidarity requires members to identify with one another and help each other because they are “one of us.” A stronger view adds shared values, loyalty, trust, and a readiness to act together. Another view says political solidarity must oppose injustice or oppression. A different account allows solidarity whenever people join together to overcome a serious difficulty, even if the problem is not political. These disagreements appear in the history of the idea. Socialists used solidarity to describe workers joining together against exploitation. Civic theories connected it with the mutual dependence of citizens and with public institutions that help people during sickness, unemployment, or old age. Nationalists connected it with a shared history and a long-term national project. Christian thinkers connected it with duties created by human dependence on one another. Social movements have asked whether solidarity should be based on a shared identity, a common experience of unfair treatment, a culture, or a political cause. Solidarity can be useful because it improves cooperation, protects members, and helps groups learn from shared experience. But critics warn that it may reduce individual freedom, spread inaccurate beliefs about what unites a group, or give insiders unfair advantages. The entry shows why solidarity is important but difficult to define and evaluate.
key_ideas: Being members of the same group is not enough for solidarity. People usually must also identify with one another and be ready to help, trust, or act together.
Some philosophers think solidarity is mainly mutual. Others think outsiders can show solidarity by supporting a disadvantaged group, especially when they listen to that group’s leadership.
Different traditions give solidarity different purposes: workers’ cooperation, citizen support, national belonging, religious duties, or resistance to injustice.
Solidarity can make group action more effective and can encourage people to protect vulnerable members.
Solidarity is not always good. A group can become unfair to outsiders, pressure members to conform, or support a harmful cause.
Social movements debate what should unite members: identity, common experiences, oppression, culture, or commitment to a shared goal.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many important changes depend on people acting together rather than separately. Solidarity helps explain how workers, citizens, and social movements organize support and challenge unfair conditions. Studying it also teaches caution: unity can be caring and powerful, but it can become exclusionary or harmful if a group ignores outsiders, silences disagreement, or pursues an unjust goal.

important_terms.definition: A strong form of unity in which people recognize a connection and are willing to support one another or act together.
Support shared by members of the same group, often involving mutual help and a willingness to put aside narrow self-interest.
Support offered to people outside the supporter’s own group; it may be one-sided rather than mutual.
People who share a social identity, experience, role, cause, or way of life and understand themselves as belonging together.
Joint activity in which people coordinate their efforts to reach a goal or overcome a problem.
The way people and institutions depend on one another, especially in a complicated society.
A situation in which a concept seems too varied or unclear to support one useful explanation.

questions_to_think_about: Is helping a stranger an act of solidarity, or is it better described as kindness or charity?
Can people disagree with one another and still have solidarity?
What should outsiders do when they want to support a movement but do not share its experiences?
Why might national or group stories sometimes leave people out?
When should duties to one’s group give way to fairness toward everyone?
